newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge says Ieng Sary should be denied pardon.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge says Ieng Sary should be denied pardon.

text.p: The mainstream Khmer Rouge urged Cambodia's king on Friday to deny a requested amnesty for dissident guerrilla leader Ieng Sary, saying he had mistreated the monarch in the past and betrayed his country.

In a radio broadcast monitored in Phnom Penh, the Khmer Rouge said Ieng Sary, who broke with hardline leader Pol Pot last month and entered peace talks with Cambodia's government, should not be granted a royal pardon from the death sentence he incurred for his role in the 1970s Khmer Rouge genocide.

The radio quoted hardline leader In Sopheap as telling a meeting of the Maoist Khmer Rouge's alternative government that an amnesty would only benefit Cambodian co-Premier Hun Sen -- a key figure in discussions on Ieng Sary's future -- and Vietnam, Cambodia's arch-enemy.
Cambodian co-premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen asked King Norodom Sihanouk on Thursday to grant Ieng Sary a pardon in the interests of peace and reconciliation.
In Sopheap, the Khmer Rouge's immigration minister, said Ieng Sary was a traitor who had sold out his people and Cambodian territory to the Vietnamese.

"No Khmer can give him amnesty. Ieng Sary always mistreated his majesty in the past and his majesty disliked him much -- how can his majesty give him amnesty?" In Sopheap told a meeting of the cabinet, which was set up in 1994 after parliament banned the group.
Several historians have written of Sihanouk's dislike for Ieng Sary, but while the king was under house arrest during much of the Khmer Rouge rule there is no evidence that he was tortured.
The date and location of the Khmer Rouge meeting were not clear.

Ieng Sary was foreign minister during the Khmer Rouge's brutal 1975-79 rule when more than one million people were executed or died of disease, starvation or exhaustion in labour camps. He was sentenced to death in absentia for his role.

After breaking away from the mainstream Khmer Rouge with several thousand followers, he asked the government to clear his legal status before continuing national reconciliation talks. Ieng Sary has also denied any responsibility for the atrocities.

King Sihanouk, whose answer on the pardon was still not known on Friday, said last month he would only consider granting an amnesty after receiving written requests from the government and a two-thirds majority of the 120-member national assembly.
An adviser to Hun Sen said the co-premiers might meet the king on Saturday to discuss the matter.

In Sopheap said the king could not grant the amnesty request, saying "Ranariddh also hates Ieng Sary as Ieng Sary tortured his father (King Sihanouk)." He said Ranariddh had only called for an amnesty under pressure from Hun Sen and Vietnam.

Hun Sen's formerly communist Cambodian People's Party was installed in power by Hanoi after Vietnamese forces ousted the Khmer Rouge in 1979. It formed a coalition with Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party after U.N.-run elections in 1993.
